title: The Ragmala
hookLine: the Granth's last page is a garland of raga names, and Sikhs hold more than one view of it

lines: THE LAST PAGE OF THE GRANTH.
cards: Two families sit down to the same holiday meal. One says the blessing one way, the other another way, both the way they always have. Nobody leaves the table.
The food is shared. The difference is just there, spoken plainly, held kindly. Sikhs have a page like that: the very last page of the Guru Granth Sahib as it is printed, called the Ragmala.
Sikhs don't all read it the same way.

teach.h: MUNDAVANI: THE SEAL ON THE BOOK.
teach.b: After the last raga, Jaijavanti, come collections of verses, then Guru Arjan's Mundavani, which tradition calls the seal on the book, where he says the dish holds truth, contentment and reflection.
Then, in the printed Granth, one more page: the Ragmala.

The name is usually read as a garland of ragas, and that's what it looks like: a list in verse naming ragas and arranging them in families, with the ragas set alongside related melodies. Here is the difference.

teach.h: SOME RECITE IT; SOME CLOSE BEFORE IT.
teach.b: Some Sikhs hold that the Ragmala belongs to the Granth as it was handed on, and recite it at the close of a complete reading.

Other Sikhs hold that it was added later, that it isn't Gurbani, the Gurus' word, and they close the reading at the Mundavani instead. Both are Sikhs, devoted to the same Guru Granth Sahib. Now the Panth's own answer.
The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the Panth's code of conduct, doesn't silence either side.
In paraphrase, it says a full reading may be concluded with the Mundavani or with the Ragmala, according to the custom of the place, and it notes that the Panth holds differing views.
It also says no copy of the Granth should be written or printed without the Ragmala.

teach.h: THE PAGE STAYS IN EVERY COPY.
teach.b: So the code keeps the page in every copy, the question stays open, and the community goes on sitting at one table.
Not every difference has to be settled to be lived with.

how: At the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, some congregations recite the Ragmala and others conclude with the Mundavani, following the custom of the place, as the Sikh Rehat Maryada allows.

practice: If you can, open the last page of the Granth online and let your eyes move slowly over the names of the ragas, reading it the way you'd read a family tree in someone else's home: with interest and with care.
Then bring to mind one person you disagree with about something that matters, and hold the difference and the person side by side, without letting go of either.
If you pray, ask in your own way for a kind heart toward them; if you don't, simply notice that both can be held at once.
